piezas.titulo: TimesJev: Thinking Fast on Time Series with System 1 Sufficiency
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2610.26002v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown strong potential for time series reasoning, while models that reason over time series are usually with long chains of thought. However, this process often consumes thousands of tokens, directly leading to substantial latency during inference. In contrast, System 1 models such as Jev make decisions instantly and can naturally be an alternative, but raw time series are not compatible with the embedding space of these models, thus hindering the reasoning performance, especially when input series contain thousands of numeric points. In this paper, we make a very early attempt to propose a time series System 1 model, namely TimesJev. Specifically, we first formalize System 1 sufficiency in time series reasoning, which motivates a compressed representation for time series with key frequency patterns preserved. To construct this representation, we derive a dimension reduction objective that combines (i) a sufficiency divergence that measures the core information lost during compression, and (ii) a realizability divergence that quantifies the incompatibility of the System 1 model to the optimal prediction given this representation. We optimize this objective by learning time series compression with a gating mechanism for sufficiency, and then aligning the selected representation with the embedding space for realizability. Finally, experiments on 13 datasets demonstrate that TimesJev outperforms reasoning models by over 62% with 62.9% less inference time than their fine-tuned versions on average.

destilado.texto: TimesJev permite razonar series temporales sin largas cadenas de pensamiento, reduciendo la latencia al comprimir los datos manteniendo patrones de frecuencia. piezas.titulo: Occupational Therapy in LGBTQ + Affirming Primary Care: Referral, Intervention, and Outcomes.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceLGBTQ + clients experience healthcare barriers that may shape daily routines, health management, and participation. Little is known about occupational therapy referral pathways and outcomes in LGBTQ + affirming primary care.ObjectiveTo describe referral characteristics, occupational performance concerns, intervention focus, and client-reported outcomes among LGBTQ + clients referred to occupational therapy.DesignRetrospective pilot program evaluation using clinical documentation and outcome data from July 2025 through March 2026, with a June 2026 analysis cutoff.SettingTwo Midwestern primary care settings where occupational therapy screening and referral processes were developed; ongoing intervention occurred through outpatient occupational therapy.ParticipantsThirty-nine referred clients were included in descriptive analyses; 38 received intervention beyond evaluation; 21 had complete baseline and follow-up Canadian Occupational Performance Measure data.InterventionIndividualized outpatient occupational therapy focused on client-identified concerns.Outcomes and MeasuresReferral and treatment characteristics, occupational performance concerns, coded occupational focus, and Canadian Occupational Performance Measure Performance and Satisfaction ratings.ResultsCommon concerns included instrumental activities of daily living (94.9%), health management/self-management (92.3%), activities of daily living (82.1%), and work or school participation (82.1%). The most common primary intervention focus was health management and chronic condition self-management (65.8%). Among participants with outcome data, COPM Performance scores improved by 2.29 points and Satisfaction scores improved by 2.58 points.Conclusions and RelevanceOccupational therapy may support LGBTQ + clients referred from primary care by addressing needs related to health management, routines, self-care, and participation through individualized outpatient intervention. Prospective multisite research is needed.

piezas.titulo: Alignment with Reflect-Reasoning: Learning How To Follow Principles
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2611.17398v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The appropriate governing norms and principles for the alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) often depend on cultural context and deployment application. However, most alignment techniques focus on training models to conform to human preferences or constitutional principles specified at training time and subsequently fixed. In practice, many deployers rely on system prompting to implement contextual norms and guardrails at inference time. Prior work has shown that post-generation reflective reasoning with critique and revision can improve conformance compared to simple system prompting, but such methods are limited to the reasoning abilities inherent in the trained model. We introduce Reflect-Reasoning, a training method that teaches models how to reason about alignment to principles, rather than simply which principles to follow. Across five models, Reflect-Reasoning consistently outperforms both system prompting and explicit prompting strategies for in-context reflective reasoning. These improvements extend and generalize to entirely out-of-distribution domains of medical and financial principles. We additionally demonstrate that Reflect-Reasoning reduces the occurrence of rare but serious principle violations. Finally, we show that Reflect-Reasoning does not erode the safety engineering of a model and is robust against jailbreaking attempts using adversarial constitutions. Overall, our results demonstrate that Reflect-Reasoning is a scalable method for training constitutional alignment as a generalizable reasoning capability, enabling models to adapt to novel principles and produce transparent reasoning traces without additional fine-tuning.

piezas.titulo: The open AI-native stack on Kubernetes: From open models to distributed inference and agents
piezas.resumenOriginal:
Over the past decade, Kubernetes established itself as the standard for orchestrating microservices and containerized applications. Today, we're witnessing the next major architectural shift in distributed computing: AI workloads moving from isolated research prototypes into large-scale, multi-tenant production fleets . In this post, we'll walk through the open-source stack that powers this shift and show you the sample manifests that you can try on your own Kubernetes clusters. You can also join us at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 to see these projects in action through live demos and technical sessions. For modern engineering teams, production AI is rapidly moving beyond generic calls to closed, black-box APIs. Organizations are realizing that their long-term competitive advantage lies in domain specialization. Platform engineers, ML researchers, and AI builders want the autonomy to run high-performing open-weight models (such as the Gemma family). They want to adapt them to proprietary enterprise datasets by using reinforcement learning (RL) and serve them with predictable latency, high throughput, and maximum hardware efficiency. Whether it's scientific initiatives training domain models like DolphinGemma (an LLM helping scientists study how dolphins communicate) on acoustic data, legal platforms evaluating complex contracts, or engineering teams building autonomous coding agents, the objective is the same: achieving frontier-level task performance at a fraction of the serving cost and latency. Yet, scaling RL post-training, stateful distributed inference, and autonomous agent execution on traditional container infrastructure introduces substantial hurdles: Accelerator underutilization in RL : When you alternate between training and rollout generation, expensive GPUs and TPUs remain idle for most of the training run. Cache-blind load balancing : When you use standard Kubernetes round-robin and least-connections routing, multi-turn agent calls are scattered across arbitrary pods and wipe out key-value (KV) cache locality. Framework fragmentation : When you operate parallel, siloed compute clusters (such as bespoke Ray or Slurm setups) alongside Kubernetes, you fragment capacity and multiply maintenance toil. Agent security in multi-tenant clusters: When you execute untrusted, model-generated shell commands and scripts in shared environments, you expose clusters to sandbox escapes and privilege escalation. At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 , Google Cloud is addressing these challenges by introducing and expanding a unified, open-source AI-native stack across Kubernetes and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) based on these components: OpenRL (CNCF Sandbox): A Kubernetes-native post training service that simplifies RL post-training and maximizes accelerator utilization. llm-d 1.0 (CNCF Sandbox): An open distributed inference control plane that provides prefix-cache-aware routing, disaggregated serving, and multi-tier KV cache management. Ray on GKE with KubeRay (CNCF Sandbox) : A framework that provides enterprise lifecycle management, elastic autoscaling, and Kueue -driven scheduling for distributed Ray compute and data processing. Agent Substrate (CNCF Sandbox) : An open orchestration runtime that provides lifecycle management and execution targets for multi-turn AI agent workflows. gVisor (CNCF Sandbox) : A kernel-level container sandbox that delivers strong system call isolation when you execute untrusted agent code in multi-tenant clusters. TorchTPU : A backend that provides first-class, native PyTorch support across Cloud TPUs and GPUs inside upstream vLLM and SGLang . Bridge reinforcement learning and Kubernetes with OpenRL While supervised fine-tuning (SFT) has become standard practice, domain excellence especially in multi-step reasoning, mathematical proofing, and autonomous tool use requires RL. Historically, it's been difficult to bridge the world of ML experimentation with production Kubernetes fleets. ML researchers want to iterate rapidly in Python and PyTorch by using standard reward functions, while platform teams need multi-tenant governance, quota enforcement, and predictable scheduling. To eliminate this friction, Google created OpenRL and contributed it to the CNCF Sandbox . Architectural highlights of OpenRL Clean 4-primitive Python abstraction : Researchers write standard Python training code that's centered around four core primitives ( forward_backward , optim_step , sample , and save_state ). OpenRL translates these primitives into Kubernetes scheduling workflows without requiring developers to learn Kubernetes internals or manage infrastructure code. Cooperative accelerator time-slicing : OpenRL interleaves training steps and rollout inferences on the same physical accelerators. This approach avoids the need to dedicate separate, static clusters to compute-bound training and latency-sensitive rollout generation. Delta-weight synchronization : Shipping full multi-gigabyte model weights over cluster networking after every optimization step creates massive network saturation. OpenRL transmits only parameter deltas to rollout workers, eliminating rollout cold starts. Zero-config dynamic resource allocation ( DRA ) : OpenRL automatically profiles model context lengths, batch dimensions, and LoRA versus full fine-tuning configurations. It then dynamically bin-packs workloads across a heterogenous accelerator fleet by using native Kubernetes DRA claims. Distributed inference at scale with llm-d 1.0 After you post-train a model, serving it serving it under interactive, bursty agent traffic presents a new set of distributed systems challenges. Standard ingress controllers treat LLM traffic as stateless HTTP requests, scattering sequential turns across different replicas and constantly rebuilding KV cache. Google Cloud, Red Hat, IBM Research, CoreWeave, and NVIDIA co-founded the project, with contributions from over 500 engineers across 25+ organizations. Today, llm-d 1.0 is the CNCF Sandbox distributed inference control plane that transforms standalone inference engines (like vLLM and SGLang) into a coordinated, cluster-wide serving fabric. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'apiVersion: inference.networking.x-k8s.io/v1alpha1

The Endpoint Picker evaluates real-time KV cache residency across worker pods. In production deployments, it's doubled KV cache hit rates from 35% to 70% and cut median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 70-85% on multi-turn agent workloads. 3-Tier KV cache offload : When accelerator high-bandwidth memory (HBM) nears capacity during long-context interactions, llm-d cascades KV cache blocks from HBM → host CPU RAM → local NVMe SSD / Google Cloud Managed Lustre / Cloud Storage. This offload prevents expensive context recalculations. DisaggregatedSet is built built on Kubernetes LeaderWorkerSet (LWS) . It enables independent horizontal scaling and coordinated, zero-downtime rolling upgrades. Native TorchTPU upstream support : PyTorch models run natively on Google Cloud TPUs inside upstream vLLM and SGLang through TorchTPU. Latency-tolerant async processing & flow control : The llm-d-async-processor component pulls background, latency-tolerant tasks from Pub/Sub or Redis into cluster slack capacity. It applies strict traffic prioritization so background processing never degrades interactive user experiences. Fleet observability with Prism : Track cluster-wide throughput, inter-token latency (ITL), TTFT, and cache hit ratios by using Prism , the llm-d open-source benchmarking and performance dashboard. Native Kueue queueing & multi-tenancy : KubeRay integrates directly with Kueue for multi-tenant fair sharing, priority preemption, and quota management across shared GPU and TPU capacity. Elastic autoscaling : KubeRay dynamically scales worker pods based on active Ray tasks and actor placement, preventing idle resource consumption. Strong isolation for AI agents: Agent Substrate & gVisor As multi-turn AI agents advance from conversational assistants to autonomous systems that generate code, execute shell commands, and orchestrate external APIs running untrusted, model-generated code in shared clusters introduces serious security risks. Google Cloud is contributing Agent Substrate and continuing core contributions to gVisor in the CNCF Sandbox: Kernel-level sandboxing : gVisor provides a user-space kernel that intercepts and virtualizes system calls, which helps ensure that untrusted agent code can't compromise the host kernel or access neighboring tenant workloads. Sub-second ephemeral execution : Sandboxes spin up in milliseconds per agent turn, providing isolated execution environments for both RL rollout generation in OpenRL and live production agent workflows. Proven in practice: Mastering domain reasoning To evaluate this complete open-source stack on a rigorous enterprise workload, we tested Gemma 4 against the open-source Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB) developed by Harvey.ai . piezas.titulo: I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper. Here’s What Happened
piezas.resumenOriginal: Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up. According to all reports, academic publishing is drowning in what has come to be called AI slop: low-quality, mass-produced content generated with AI. By 2025, an estimated 57 percent of all published academic articles exhibited detectable evidence of large language model (LLM) influence, a massive jump from 12 percent in 2023. What’s more, over 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews were found to be completely AI-generated in 2025. Given that for every 40 papers showing statistical evidence of AI usage in 2025, only one formally disclosed it , these figures likely grossly underestimate LLM involvement today. Of course, evidence of AI use doesn’t necessarily mean a paper is slop. But some estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated, publications are now produced annually. “It’s not just the [scientific] record under threat, it’s science as a whole,” warns Amanda Sulicz , IEEE’s research-integrity manager. “AI slop is completely eroding trust in science and every scientific process that we’ve worked for centuries to create.” Yet statistics and statements claiming that the problem is big—perhaps even existential for science—don’t really get the message across. Just how easy is it to use AI to create a convincing but completely fake paper? And without adding even more to the burden on stretched peer reviewers, who do this work on a volunteer basis, do publishers have the tools to keep AI slop out of the scientific record? Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney , managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access , if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed. The experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research? Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system. Round 1: Creating the Forgery To give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone. I assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape. My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. And it highlighted a recurring problem during the process: Without any real research to work with, the output was laughably thin, with the LLMs often struggling to fill four pages. However, as I became more adept at prompting the models, they loosened up and became more characteristically loquacious. I broke the paper down into its constituent parts—abstract, introduction, methods, and so on—and tackled them one by one. If one LLM refused to go any further, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like “hypothetically” would often do the trick. After a dozen or so prompts, I had a realistic-looking paper. A dozen or so more prompts generated and tidied up the figures and captions, produced references and citations, and converted the paper into IEEE Access ’s required style. At this point, I read the full paper carefully. To me, it looked pretty good. The science sounded convincing. I even had visions of returning to academia to conduct in real life the experiments that the LLMs had proposed. What’s more, I couldn’t see any obvious telltale “AI-isms” that would immediately be flagged. For example, the LLMs didn’t produce any tortured phrases—unusual paraphrases of standard technical terms, like “profound neural organization” replacing “deep neural network.” Other AI-isms were arguably present, involving stylistic tics like hedging language (“potentially, typically”), grouping things in threes (“The study provides a clear, concise, and actionable framework”), and inserting formulaic transitions (“In summary,…”). But as the previous sentence demonstrates, these tics are hard to spot because they are often used by unimaginative humans, too. Round 1: Attempt to Publish Two Ways to Make a Paper With AI I took two very different routes to creating a scientific paper with AI. First, I coaxed free, general-purpose chatbots through the process step by step; then I turned to FARS, an autonomous research system designed to do much of the scientific work itself. ROUND 1: CHATGPT + GEMINI 1. Choose a research topic I ask the free chatbots to create an original paper on optical solitons, my former Ph.D. field. 2. Break the paper into pieces The initial results are thin, so I prompt separately for the abstract, introduction, methods, and other sections. 3. Keep steering the LLMs When one model refuses or stalls, I switch models, rephrase prompts, and ask what the next step would look like “hypothetically.” 4. Build and polish the paper After about two dozen prompts, the LLMs have generated the text, figures, captions, references, and citations and formatted the paper for IEEE Access . 5. Put it to the test I send the fake paper to IEEE Access , where automated integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references. → CAUGHT IEEE’s integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references. ROUND 2: FARS 1. Give FARS a research topic I enter an abbreviated version of the same optical-soliton topic. FARS generates a research proposal in 21 minutes. 2. Authorize the experiment With a click, I tell FARS to carry out the experiment described in its proposal. 3. Let FARS do the research FARS conducts the computational experiment and emails me the next day to say it’s complete. 4. Tell FARS to write the paper Without checking the results, I click “Write paper.” Two hours later, FARS produces a submission-ready article. 5. Put it to the test I remove FARS’s disclosure, put my name on the paper, and send it to IEEE Access . → CAUGHT The references are real, but IEEE flags the paper’s heavy reliance on non-peer-reviewed preprints. Handing the fake paper over to IEEE Access left me torn. After putting in a fair amount of effort into making the AI-generated forgery, would I be happy if it passed through the checkers, or saddened that the only remaining line of defense for publishers is the evermore-burdened peer-review community? And if it was spotted, would I be angry that I didn’t think of a red flag or be glad the checkers did their job? As it turned out, I was filled with relief when the paper got picked up quickly for having hallucinated references, otherwise known as ghost citations. When I ran the paper through Gemini afterward, without qualm it happily reported that seven “modern LLM-related research references have been fabricated to support the paper’s specific narrative.” Thanks for the heads up, Gemini! In fact, Gemini underestimated how many ghost citations there were. When Mahoney ran the paper through a research-integrity checker called STM Integrity Hub , she picked up 12, and another checker from MolecularConnections could not validate 24 references, including one that had the classic tell of “John Smith” as a single author (no offense to all the academically inclined John Smiths out there). “I am an experimental physicist by training, so this was not at all my area, but nothing seemed majorly scientifically wrong ” about the paper, says Mahoney. “It was just that so many hallucinated references immediately cast doubt on the entire work.” Feedback on the fake paper from Gaetano Assanto , an expert in optical solitons and a former collaborator of mine from Roma Tre University, in Italy, was similarly mixed. Concentrating on the paper itself, he thought it looked professionally written. But he noted that the mathematics was very dense (“too much math for me in a single shot!”) and would require specialized knowledge to evaluate. And, although the text looked legitimate, Assanto noted an excessive use of acronyms in the abstract, and he was suspicious of a couple of confidently proclaimed physics statements that were at best debatable. The AI Arms Race On one level, this outcome was positive: A complete novice using free tools couldn’t get an AI-faked paper past the publishers’ automated defenses or a potential peer reviewer’s eagle eye. But it was hardly a resounding victory for the scientific publishing system. With general-purpose LLMs and no special prompting expertise, I had managed to conjure a superficially plausible scientific paper out of research that had never happened. And more advanced LLMs are no longer making the kind of mistakes their free, dumber relatives are making. These tools aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us. It’s common knowledge in the academic publishing world that, in the cat-and-mouse game between bad actors and publishers, AI slop papers continue to slip through publishers’ safeguards. “It feels like building a detection tool today may not be effective with the AI-created paper of tomorrow,” says Luigi Longobardi , IEEE’s director of publishing ethics and conduct. This leaves the humble peer reviewer as a publisher’s last line of defense. Yet peer review is simply not fit to handle the volume of papers—both legitimate and slop—passing through. Even before AI tools became ubiquitous, the peer-review system was being pushed to its breaking point, processing well over 3 million papers in 2022. Fundamentally, this problem stems from science’s publish-or-perish culture, which pressures academics to constantly publish papers in prestigious journals to secure funding and advance their careers. This culture not only forces many academics to regularly churn out incremental research, but has also long driven some to enlist the help of “paper mills”—unethical organizations that produce low-quality or fabricated papers—just to keep pace. AI only amplifies these existing dynamics. Burden on Academics Mahoney says IEEE Access alone receives about 60,000 submissions per year, accepting around 20 percent, or about 12,000 papers. Every accepted paper is reviewed by at least two independent reviewers. But despite the journal’s roster of tens of thousands of peer reviewers, it’s getting harder and harder to secure their services, with the average number of reviewer invitations being sent out for each article increasing by 50 percent since 2018. For these volunteers, peer review is a significant commitment on top of teaching and conducting their own research. Now they’re also being asked to spot AI slop. Of course, peer review is not the end of scrutiny for any paper. Once it has entered the scientific record, it must then pass muster with the scientific community. This is where thousands of papers with telltale signs of inappropriate AI use (and other forms of research misconduct) have been exposed. What Gave Away My AI Papers Round 1: The Fake Paper Created with free versions of ChatGPT and Gemini Ghost citations Many references were fabricated or couldn’t be validated. Questionable scientific claims An expert flagged confidently stated claims that were at best debatable. Too many acronyms The expert also noted excessive use of acronyms in the abstract. Round 2: The AI-Research Paper Created by the autonomous research system FARS Too many preprints The references were real, but too many pointed to non-peer-reviewed preprints. Nonsense in a figure One technical figure contained a line labeled “lhewl.” AI artifacts Another figure’s depiction of an AI “brain” contained telltale random dots. There are two high-profile homes for this important and completely volunteer-led post-publication review work. PubPeer is a place where researchers, often called scientific sleuths, can anonymously identify flaws in the literature. And Retraction Watch documents and publicizes corrections to the scientific record. Even the people who track problems in the scientific literature can find themselves caught up in AI fabrications. Ivan Oransky , cofounder of Retraction Watch and a member of the PubPeer Foundation’s board of directors, has encountered papers containing fabricated references attributed to him. In one case, a journal article criticizing post-publication peer review included a fabricated reference supposedly written by Oransky himself—“which was sort of funny,” he chuckles. Oransky argues that AI has exposed long-standing weaknesses in the scientific publishing system rather than creating an entirely new problem: “What I liken it to is a fire, where publish-or-perish has always been there as kindling, paper mills are the gasoline, and AI is the accelerant.” But though concerning, the crisis could create an opportunity, he says. “If I’m trying to be optimistic, maybe AI slop and the volume of submissions could make more people aware of those problems and try and solve them at a fundamental first-principles level.” Blurred Lines My homemade forgery had failed for reasons that today’s publishers know how to spot. But that raised a more unsettling question: What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication? Making my vibe-researched paper look like a cave drawing, new automated research systems are handing increasingly large parts of the scientific process over to AI. Tools including FARS (Fully Automated Research System) , AutoResearchClaw , The AIScientist-v2 , Zochi , AI Researcher , and DeepScientist all aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us. What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication? Often with just a single prompt, these AI engines can conduct a comprehensive literature search, from which they can generate a completely reasonable research proposal. They can design and conduct experiments using digital datasets and simulations and then write a full research paper—all with no human input after the initial prompt. Very recent systems are even beginning to go beyond the digital realm. LabClaw , for example, now links to autonomous labs that can generate real-world data for tasks such as drug discovery. The output is, to most intents and purposes, actual research, and therefore potentially worthy of publication. But with humans in the loop in only the most nominal sense, these tools bring into question the meaning of the term “legitimate science.” FARS, which caused a stir this year when it created 166 papers in 417 hours , was developed by the Singapore-based startup Analemma . “We built FARS because research is still constrained by human attention, fragmented tools, scarce technical labor, and slow experimental iteration,” explains Xiwen Su , Analemma’s manager of product operations and partnerships. “FARS can pursue many research threads simultaneously, 24/7, without fatigue, and at scale.” (The online service that I used to access FARS was discontinued after Analemma was acquired by Baidu while this article was being reported.) Su and the team behind Analemma kindly agreed to let me loose on FARS and gave me enough credits to create a paper. Which gave me another opportunity to put Mahoney’s research-integrity checkers to the test. Round 2: Using an AI Science Engine FARS is not an LLM in and of itself, but rather an agentic AI-orchestration system connected to a computing cluster that has access to essentially any open- or closed-source LLM it needs. The system uses four specialized agents for ideation, planning, conducting the experiment, and writing, all designed to perform the main tasks of science autonomously. Though FARS initially focused on AI research, Su told me it should be reasonably effective across other domains. As I wanted a topic similar to that of my first fake paper, I pasted in an abridged version of that paper’s title—“LLM-aided Optical Soliton Dynamics Modelling for Next-Gen Communications”—into the prompt box and hit “Send.” Just 21 minutes later, FARS generated a research proposal based on an extremely detailed literature review—far more than I or any other human could have achieved in that time. With a click, I tasked FARS with conducting the experiment it detailed in its research proposal. The next day, I received an email saying my experiment was complete. Without checking the results, I pressed a button marked “Write paper,” and the final submission-ready article was produced in 2 hours. At this point, I finally had a look at some of the output. At first glance, the paper looked convincingly human-written. The only giveaway was a line just below the abstract reading: “WARNING: This paper was generated by an automated research system.” I deleted that, put my name in its place, and sent it to Mahoney. Round 2: Attempt to Publish Because FARS is designed to spot gaps in the scientific literature and conduct real research to close them, I was more confident it would breeze through the publisher’s checks. But just as my fake paper fell down in the references, so too did the AI-generated real one. “Your fake article had lots of hallucinated references,” says Mahoney. “While this AI-generated one had no fake references, our team would have rejected this paper because it did have a huge percentage of references to preprints, which likely has something to do with the dataset the AI has access to.” Because preprints haven’t yet undergone peer review, IEEE Access considers heavy reliance on them a problem. In addition, although the research-integrity checking tools didn’t spot any issues with figures, Mahoney did. One figure included a red line labeled with the nonsense term “lhewl,” and an AI “brain” in another figure had some random dots in it, which ironically were a tell that it was AI generated. Automation Changing the Landscape Automated research systems are very much a work in progress, but they are already starting to make waves in the scientific community. For instance, an AI Scientist academic paper and papers from the Autoscience Institute were accepted through double-blind peer review in 2025 by the International Conference on Learning Representations. As these systems improve and start to produce research outputs at volume, the waves are likely to build to a tsunami that will threaten today’s scientific and publishing process. “FARS doesn’t kill the paper, but it does challenge the paper as the unit of knowledge ,” argues Su. “We believe the future looks more like a living knowledge graph—where individual, well-scoped contributions (some made by humans, some by machines) connect and build on each other dynamically.” In this future, humans will continue to have roles in the scientific and publication processes—just very different and limited ones. For example, instead of conducting experiments themselves, humans would sense-check and review automated output at key points. And traditional line-by-line peer-reviewing will be a thing of the past, though Su emphasizes that this change will not eliminate human judgment. “Automated systems can handle reproducibility checks, statistical validation, and novelty screening,” she says. “Humans can then focus on the harder question: Does this [research] matter?” A Human-Centric or AI-Driven Future? Though from a very different world than Su, Mahoney agrees that humans need to be freed to focus on the science, and that technology holds the key. “It’s promising to see the progress that has been made to automate some of the triage tasks, such as author checks, tortured phrases, duplicate submission, reference validity, et cetera,” she says. “During peer review, we’re also using AI semantic search tools to help editors match manuscripts to the most relevant reviewers, who are best placed to stop the slop before entering the scientific record.” In addition, Mahoney thinks that AI cannot be banned or overly restricted, as this will stymie progress at a time when human knowledge could and should be growing at an unprecedented rate. “Researchers are increasingly using AI in their work, from literature discovery, to code generation, to data analysis, and this is not necessarily a bad thing,” she argues. But she disagrees that peer reviewers and humans more broadly will play a smaller part in scientific progress; Mahoney believes the future still requires humans at the wheel. The question is not just whether the research matters, she says. “The question should be: Can this work be trusted and reproduced?” To this end, Longobardi argues that AI may ultimately require scientists to prove not just what they discovered but how they discovered it. One possibility, he says, is using technology to verify research at the source. “The system doesn’t really help because it’s not designed to not trust the paper,” he explains. “Maybe institutions can think about developing their own trust markers, automatically integrating the equipment researchers use with blockchain technology to say ‘Yes, this person was in the lab on this day and got this data.’” Elements of this approach are already emerging. For instance, two departments within the Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces have implemented a sample database, assigning each and every sample created under their roofs with a unique ID and QR code. And the University of Southampton’s School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering has rolled out an electronic lab notebook system. These innovative safeguards represent early efforts toward keeping humans front and center in scientific progress, and making the scientific process itself more transparent. Whether this human-centric vision, Su’s AI-driven aspiration, or some other picture of the future wins out remains to be seen. The one thing my vibe-research adventure has clarified is that business-as-usual science is not an option. Scientists and publishers must adapt to a world in which it’s becoming increasingly difficult to spot the difference between real research and AI forgeries, and where deciding what counts as legitimate scientific work may become even harder than detecting outright fraud. Paper 1: The AI-Generated Forgery Created with ChatGPT and Gemini, this paper describes research that never happened. Paper 2: The AI-Generated Research Paper Created with Analemma’s FARS system, this paper describes computational research conducted by AI. Neither paper was peer reviewed, and their scientific claims have not been independently validated.

piezas.titulo: Relationship Between Spine Deformity and Motor Control With Neurosensory Asymmetry in Patients With Lenke Type 1 Scoliosis - A Pilot Study.
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundIn patients with idiopathic scoliosis, the spinal deformity influences internal mass distribution. These patients have no neurological, muscular disturbance or any other diseases. However, modern research reveals subtle central nervous system and sensory differences when comparing patients to healthy controls, with a malfunction of the vestibular system and sensory integration. Motor control asymmetry between the left and right sides may exaggerate the differences in mass distribution as a function of spinal curvature, particularly in patients with a single thoracic curvature.PurposeThis study, focusing on adolescents with idiopathic Lenke type 1 scoliosis, aimed to define the relationship between spine deformity and low motor control and to describe the asymmetry of motor control between the left and right sides.MethodWe performed a retrospective study of 17 patients with idiopathic Lenke type 1-curve scoliosis who performed a dynamic equilibrium test in eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions.ResultsGreater curvature was found to be associated with a greater imbalance, corresponding to weaker motor control. The correlation was significant in the eyes-open condition (r 2 = 0.76; p 2 = 0.34; p = .13). An effect of side was observed, with a significantly greater median center-of-mass frequency on the side contralateral to the spinal deformities ( p = .03).ConclusionThe median center-of-mass frequency between the ipsilateral and contralateral sides revealed neurosensory asymmetry in these patients. This asymmetry was not correlated with spinal deformity and appeared to depend on visual information.

piezas.titulo: Beyond Source Code: Evaluating Natural Language Specifications for LLM-Based C-to-Rust Translation
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2611.17581v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promising results for C-to-Rust translation, yet existing approaches primarily rely on source code as input, leaving natural-language specifications of program behavior underexplored as an alternative or complementary representation. We hypothesize that direct code translation encourages LLMs to preserve C-specific implementation choices, producing Rust that may be functionally correct but unnecessarily verbose, reliant on unsafe constructs, and less idiomatic. We investigate this hypothesis by comparing three translation settings: code-only, specification-only, and code-and-specification. Using 300 C programs from the IBM CodeNet dataset, we evaluate GPT-5.2 and GPT-4o-mini on functional correctness, maintainability, complexity, idiomaticity, unsafe construct usage, and cost. Code-only translation achieves the highest test pass rate (98.6%) but often mirrors C's implementation patterns. In contrast, specification-only translation produces the most idiomatic and compact Rust, reducing unsafe blocks by approximately 6x and Clippy style warnings by 2.4x. However, using specifications without validation yields test pass rates as low as 86% with our best performing model. Adding an iterative test-based validation and refinement step for specifications raises this to a 95.3% test pass rate. Overall, specification-based translation consistently improves code quality relative to code-only translation, while code-and-specification offers the best balance between correctness (98.3% test pass rate) and maintainability. Our study systematically compares these translation settings, highlighting the trade-offs among specification quality, translation correctness, code quality, and computational cost.

Mim has taught both university level (California State-Dominguez Hills) and professional continuing education courses since 2013, spoken internationally, and has co-authored works for professional publications. She has been in her current role at STAR Institute since 2017 at the invitation of Dr. Lucy Jane Miller, PhD, FAOTA, OTR. Gina’s practice is rooted in attachment and systems theories, making her truly a relationally focused therapist. As such, she believes that our greatest healing occurs in the context of relationships. She has always been oriented toward a biopsychosocial approach to her theory of change, thereby honoring the importance of the mind-body connection. She believes that within a safe space and through our attuned relationship with Self and others, we all have the power to tune into our instinct towards healing. With her early career in occupational therapy, Gina has incredible understanding of the importance of self-determination for clients: competence, autonomy, and relatedness. Gina was drawn to couples and family therapy for its non-pathologizing approach to viewing clients’ problems. Gina is especially equipped to support neurodivergent individuals, couples and families, as well as those navigating issues around disability and chronic illness. She is capable of easily moving between deep therapeutic work, parent coaching and individual skills training - making her a versatile therapist. She has experience supporting clients with life transitions, anxiety, depression, non-suicidal self-harm, suicidal ideation, recovery from adverse childhood experiences and trauma, developing deeper emotional awareness, identifying and leaving behind maladaptive coping patterns, and improving self-esteem. piezas.titulo: Fragments: November 10
piezas.resumenOriginal: It’s that time of the year when the November Thoughtworks Technology Radar appears. Again my colleagues have taken a sweep of the technologies that our teams have used in the field, and pulled together a summary of what’s popped up in the last six months. It’s been a busy half-year, one that again has been dominated by AI, and that’s reflected in the many AI blips on the radar. The mass of blips makes it hard to develop a coherent story around trends, but Chris Ford has done a fine job of the writing the accompanying article on macro trends . One team of passionate people experimenting with agents can make almost anything work. They share a context, a credit card and a mental model. They review each other’s work because they sit together, and they know what to check and how much latitude to give the coding agent. Two hundred people, though, cannot work that way. The moment agentic AI becomes an operating model rather than a pilot, a second layer of problems appears: How is context shared between teams? What’s the token bill? How do we deal with increased review demands? What’s the agent allowed to reach, read and change? And who’s now responsible for the harness everyone depends on? Experience so far suggests that the questions that enterprises face are about: shared context, token cost, cognitive load, security, and platform building. While these issues are distinct, they are not separate, so strategies to answer them must take all of them into account. I also echo Chris in reminding us that however impressive these tools are, we must remember that while we have to rethink systems and workflows to utilize these technologies, they should be built to serve humans - and we should all benefit from its bounty. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Ben Thompson’s Stratechery newsletter reflects on the recent election’s impact on data centers . I watch a lot of sports, and particularly this fall, watched a lot of baseball. My Milwaukee Brewers — excuse me, my World Champion Milwaukee Brewers — demanded my full attention, which also meant I saw a lot of campaign ads, and by far the most common topic, at least here in Wisconsin, was data centers. Moreover, it was never entirely clear which way it cut politically: both parties were anti-data center, accusing their opponent of being the opposite. He points out that this opposition is recent, and tied to a shift in focus from the internet and streaming movies to AI: you know, the technology that in the best case scenario is going to take everyone’s jobs, and in the worst case scenario end the human race. There’s going to be a lot said about how Democratic officials will be at the heart of blocking data center building, but as his point above about campaign ads illustrates, the opposition to data centers is (at least at the moment) a bi-partisan opposition. He follows up with “ten takes” from these consequences. The big beneficiaries of this opposition to building data centers will be those who own the data centers that have already been built. The opposition will reduce supply of tokens, meaning that token costs will go up, thus increasing the profits for those who already have their token generators plugged in and humming. There’s also benefits to those who aren’t constrained by the need to build more big data centers. Other countries aren’t affected by a change in US policy, China is the most talked-about case here, but it’s not the only country that may benefit from a drop in US data center building. Apple may also benefit, if it means more AI work is pushed to edge devices that are their territory, in addition to having not sunk so many dollars into AI-specific investments. To his analysis, I’ll add that this may also have a somewhat counter-intuitive effect on regulation, and corporate attitudes to it. The common expectation is that businesses are opposed to government regulation, since that interferes with their free pursuit of profit. That’s true to an extent, but it’s quite common to see established businesses lobby (quietly) in favor of regulation that acts as a barrier to new competitors. So I wouldn’t be at all surprised to see companies that have already built data centers to be pushing for regulations that impede or prevent new ones from being built. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I’ve been a long-time fan of Hadley Wickham, for how he has tamed the rather messy world of R programming into a well-designed tidyverse . He is another thoughtful voice to listen to as we move into the world of agentic engineering , in this case by trying to figure out what the real cost of tokens is . I hear a lot of suspicion that AI tokens are unsustainably priced and that frontier labs are heavily subsidising costs with their VC money. They want to get us hooked now, so they can pull the rug out from under us whenever they want to make a bunch of money. Is that true? My sense is that it’s mostly not. But can I back that up with some data? His conclusion is that it doesn’t seem that token costs are significantly subsidized on per-token API basis, but they are with subscription plans. (He caveats his analysis, saying it doesn’t take into account recouping the costs of training the models.) ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ There’s a creepy excitement at the thought that models are clever enough to edit the weights of models, an activity that Takehi et al refer to as Weight-Space Programming . Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. While we don’t know if we’ll ever be able to download skills directly into our brains ( “I know kung fu” - or for those in my particular demographic: Joe 90 ), this does raise the possibility of downloading capabilities into models by manipulating their weights. Simon Wilison riffed on this paper by examining whether an LLM can understand model behaviors from the weights alone , by examining four simple neural networks, each trained to play a specific game, and figuring out which game it was by just looking at the weights. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Jessica Kerr (jessitron): My days of teaching AI to do stuff are numbered. Getting it to teach me stuff is more fun. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Houck et al (that “al” includes some folks who I’ve learned to pay a lot of attention to), look at how we can assess the quality of context supplied to agents. An agent may draw from source code, specifications, issue trackers, chat histories, architectural documents, tool output, and user instructions, then act on that combination with limited human supervision. Information that was written for different audiences, at different times, and for different purposes is brought together into a temporary operating environment for a particular task. Whether each source is individually useful does not reveal whether the resulting context is fit for the work the agent is being asked to do. They’ve come up with a framework for describing the quality of this assembled context , which they refer to as CAFE(S). The acronym refers to five dimensions they look at: Clarity: Can the agent interpret the request as intended? Actionability: Can the agent proceed, and know when it is done? Fidelity: Can the agent trust that this context is true? Efficiency: Can the agent focus on what matters? Security: Should the agent have this context at all? They also list a set of half-a-dozen “context smells”: common cases where these break down (and a nod to Kent’s original metaphor ) I’m not sure about the name, (how exactly should I pronounce “CAFE(S)”?) and the article exhibits rather more LLM Voice that I prefer. But on the whole I think this is a good framing for thinking about an important part of feeding our silicon servants/overlords. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Cindy Sridharan noted that the problems she ran into six months ago are no longer around : What was missing in my setup 6 months ago was the verification process I now use. 70% of my daily token spend goes into verifying patches, and only ~20-30% into creating them. That resonated with conversations I’ve had with folks using agents in enterprise settings. They are using far more tokens to check the working of models (through guardrails and evals) than they are to generate a response to a request. A single request to a model from a customer may trigger a dozen turns to other models to probe its input and verify its output.

piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundCheek-puff weakness is clinically recognised in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), but its relation to non-invasive facial electrophysiology is uncertain.ObjectiveThe primary objective was to test whether participant-level orbicularis oris motor unit number index (MUNIX) was lower in ALS than in healthy controls after age and sex adjustment. Secondary and exploratory objectives related cheek-puff weakness to facial MUNIX, nerve conduction, blink reflex, and onset phenotype.MethodsIn this retrospective cross-sectional study, we analysed 43 patients with ALS, 25 healthy controls (Control A), and 42 peripheral vestibular disease controls (Control B).ResultsThe adjusted primary MUNIX difference versus Control A was not significant (β = −7.08; p = 0.153). Cheek-puff weakness was more frequent than eye-closure weakness (21/43 versus 4/43; exact McNemar p < 0.001) and was associated with lower orbicularis oris MUNIX after age and sex adjustment (β = −13.09; p = 0.006). In limb-onset ALS, cheek-puff weakness remained associated with lower MUNIX after additional adjustment (β = −17.40, 95% confidence interval −30.56 to −4.25; p = 0.011); only nine patients had bulbar-onset ALS, limiting comparison between onset groups. Orbicularis oris distal motor latency remained longer after adjustment (p = 0.011), and R2 was abnormal in 11/39 patients versus 0/42 Control B participants (p < 0.001).ConclusionAssessment of cheek puff and eye closure is relevant irrespective of ALS onset site. piezas.titulo: An EMG-driven virtual reality platform for physiology-based motor interaction: technical and functional validation
piezas.resumenOriginal: Harnessing experience-dependent neuroplasticity has become a central goal of modern neurorehabilitation. Immersive virtual reality (VR) has emerged as a promising tool, enabling task-oriented training in ecologically valid scenarios that are difficult to reproduce in conventional clinical settings. Despite these advances, interaction in most existing VR rehabilitation systems remains primarily mediated by external interfaces, such as motion tracking or handheld controllers, rather than by the user’s own physiological motor activity. Consequently, rehabilitation often fails to directly engage the physiological motor commands that naturally drive voluntary movement. We present and validate an integrated VR–electromyography (VR-EMG) platform that enables closed-loop, physiology-driven interaction between users and immersive virtual environments. The platform combines a standalone VR architecture with wearable EMG systems, online EMG decoding, and cloud-based performance monitoring within a unified framework. A standardized motor-command interface enables different EMG acquisition systems to control both anthropomorphic and non-anthropomorphic virtual effectors without modifying the decoding strategy or rehabilitation scenarios, providing a flexible framework for diverse applications. The platform was validated through complementary technical and functional evaluations performed on the two supported EMG acquisition systems. Technical validation assessed signal quality, gesture classification accuracy, communication latency, and system reliability. Functional validation was conducted in individuals with upper-limb amputation and able-bodied controls while performing object-interaction tasks across multiple immersive virtual scenarios. The platform demonstrated stable closed-loop operation, reliable gesture recognition, and the ability to quantify objective performance metrics, including task score, completion time, gesture classification errors, precision errors, correctly recognized gestures, and user-reported workload. Findings demonstrate the feasibility, technical reliability, and functional versatility of the proposed platform by providing a physiology-driven framework for immersive motor interaction that is compatible with different EMG acquisition systems and dissociates motor control from the morphology of the controlled virtual effector. Because the two systems were used for different components of the validation, we do not establish equivalence in their performance. By integrating online EMG decoding, VR, and quantitative performance monitoring, the platform offers a tool for future applications in rehabilitation, prosthetic training, and studies using functional magnetic resonance imaging and high-density electroencephalography to address whether training with the platform induces changes in functional brain organization.

piezas.titulo: Neuronal Aralar/AGC1 deficiency impairs social behavior through dopaminergic and redox dysfunction and is rescued by β-hydroxybutyrate
piezas.resumenOriginal: Background: Pathogenic variants in SLC25A12/AGC1 (Aralar) have been linked to autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet the mechanisms connecting neuronal metabolic dysfunction to altered social behavior remain poorly understood. Aralar is a key component of the malate-aspartate shuttle, supporting neuronal oxidative metabolism and lactate utilization. Here, we investigated the consequences of postnatal neuronal Aralar deletion and the therapeutic potential of {beta}-hydroxybutyrate (BHB). Methods: We generated neuron-specific Aralar knockout mice (Neu Aralar-KO) using CamKII-Cre, producing efficient recombination in cortex, hippocampus, and striatum. Behavioral, transcriptomic, neurochemical, morphometric, histological, and biochemical analyses were performed in adult mice. The effects of systemic BHB administration were assessed using behavioral, metabolic, oxidative stress, and transcriptomic endpoints. Results: Despite a 55-65% reduction of Aralar expression in forebrain regions, Neu Aralar-KO mice displayed normal growth, survival, brain structure, and myelination. Unexpectedly, loss of neuronal Aralar did not impair spatial memory, episodic memory, or reversal learning. In contrast, Neu Aralar-KO mice exhibited hyperactivity and a marked deficit in sociability, revealing an ASD-relevant behavioral phenotype. Morphological analysis showed significant remodeling of striatal dendritic spines without changes in spine density. Transcriptomic profiling identified 433 differentially expressed genes, the vast majority being upregulated, with enrichment of pathways related to neuropeptide signaling, synaptic transmission, membrane excitability, and behavior. Notably, genes involved in dopamine (DA) and glutamate handling, synaptic connectivity, neuromodulatory signaling, and ASD-associated pathways were strongly induced. Neurochemical analyses revealed preserved glutamate and GABA levels but reduced striatal DA content accompanied by an increased DOPAC/DA ratio, indicating enhanced DA degradation. DAergic neurons of the ventral tegmental area (VTA) showed minimal recombination, suggesting that DA dysfunction arises through non-cell-autonomous mechanisms. Consistent with increased DA oxidative catabolism, Neu Aralar-KO striata displayed elevated lipid peroxidation, induction of glutathione-related pathways, upregulation of antioxidant genes, and astrocyte activation. Remarkably, BHB treatment restored sociability, normalized striatal metabolic alterations, reduced oxidative stress, and abolished genotype-dependent neurochemical abnormalities. Transcriptomic analyses further revealed that Aralar deficiency recapitulates a substantial fraction of the fasting/BHB-induced epigenetic transcriptional program. Conclusions: Postnatal neuronal Aralar deficiency uncouples social behavior from cognitive performance and drives ASD-like phenotypes through a mechanism linking neuronal metabolic dysfunction, oxidative stress, glial activation, and impaired DAergic homeostasis. The rescue of behavioral, metabolic, and redox abnormalities by BHB identifies restoration of metabolic homeostasis as a major therapeutic mechanism and highlights metabolic interventions as promising strategies for AGC1 deficiency and ASD-associated disorders involving neuronal metabolic dysfunction.

piezas.titulo: Frequency-specific cortical swallowing-network responses following neuroengineering-guided individualized multichannel tDCS.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Background Neuromodulatory interventions for dysphagia are increasingly explored as adjunctive rehabilitation strategies, yet their efficacy may be limited by non-individualized stimulation protocols and insufficient consideration of network-specific brain dynamics. Advances in neuroengineering now enable individualized targeting based on functional neuroimaging and computational modeling, offering the potential for precision neuromodulation of swallowing-related brain networks. Methods We investigated whether individualized multichannel transcranial direct current stimulation (mc-tDCS), optimized using magnetoencephalography (MEG)-derived target localization, MRI-based finite-element head modeling, and a distributed constrained maximum intensity (D-CMI) optimization framework, modulates the cortical swallowing network. In a randomized sham-controlled crossover design, eight healthy adults underwent three stimulation conditions: low-intensity mc-tDCS (1.5 mA), high-intensity mc-tDCS (4.0 mA), and sham stimulation. Swallowing-related cortical activity was assessed before and after stimulation using MEG source reconstruction of event-related desynchronization during uncued voluntary swallowing and a visually cued swallowing task requiring precise timing. A repeated-measures Dose × Task × Time model tested the hypothesized interaction separately in five frequency bands, with Holm correction across bands. Results No Dose × Task × Time interaction was significant after Holm correction across the five frequency bands (all adjusted p ≥ 0.274). Within-condition pre-post analyses identified alpha- and beta-band changes after 1.5-mA stimulation during challenged swallowing and a low-gamma change after 4.0-mA stimulation during uncued swallowing. Challenged-task timing accuracy increased over time, without significant Dose or Dose × Time effects. Conclusions This study demonstrates the feasibility of integrating individualized MEG-based targeting, subject-specific head modeling, and optimized multichannel stimulation. The hypothesized Dose × Task × Time interaction was not significant. Exploratory within-condition pre-post differences were observed in alpha, beta, and low-gamma activity, but do not establish stimulation-specific effects. Larger controlled studies are needed to evaluate the physiological effects of this individualized approach.

piezas.resumenOriginal: Vision and proprioception are the 2 primary senses integrated to plan and execute upper-limb movements. Virtual reality technology enables the investigation of population-level differences in vision-proprioception integration during a shoulder joint position sense test within a 3-dimensional environment by dissociating vision from proprioception through visual hand offsets. A total of 122 participants (collegiate baseball and softball players and age-, sex-, and throwing side-matched healthy controls) performed a shoulder joint position sense test under accurate and offset visual feedback conditions in virtual reality. Participants demonstrated significantly more negative joint repositioning constant error and larger absolute error under offset vision compared with accurate vision (P .05). The mean vision-proprioception reliance score across all groups was 0.9, with 0 to 1 as the theoretical bounds, indicating strong dominance of vision over proprioception. These findings suggest that when both vision and proprioception are available, individuals across populations exhibit comparable repositioning errors through vision dominant integration. Future studies should further examine proprioception-dominant or sport-specific tasks, such as baseball catching or hitting, to clarify population and limb-side differences in multisensory integration mechanisms.

piezas.titulo: Sensory Processing Differences in Children With Idiopathic Toe Walking: A Scoping Review and Exploratory Meta-Analysis.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceThe cause of idiopathic toe walking (ITW) remains unclear, though impaired sensory processing has often been hypothesized to be linked to ITW.ObjectivesThe objective of this article is to review the literature on toe-walking to identify how sensory processing contributes to ITW.Data SourcesFour databases (CINAHL, Pubmed, PsychINFO, and SCOPUS) were searched for papers related to sensory processing and ITW published prior to July 2024. References of retrieved papers were reviewed for additional sources.Study Selection and Data CollectionThe PRISMA guidelines for scoping review were used to abstract the data following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology. Inclusion criteria were examined and papers included at least one sensory system related to ITW was studied. Papers were excluded if toe walking was due to diagnosed neurological, orthopedic, or genetic conditions.FindingsOur scoping review identified 13 published articles relevant to examining sensory processing in children with ITW. Studies explored differences in vibration perception, light touch, proprioception, vestibular, visual processing, sensorimotor functional assessments, and parental surveys of sensory processing. Six of the papers were included in a meta-analysis on vibration perception threshold that failed to reach significance ( p = .12). Despite heterogeneity across studies in participants, methods, and outcomes, a meta-analysis for atypical scores from parent-report sensory processing survey data yielded significant differences between children with ITW and typical controls ( p < .0068).Conclusions and RelevanceChildren with ITW demonstrate impairments across multiple domains of sensory processing and sensory-motor function suggesting an underlying relationship between ITW and sensory differences. Children with ITW, however, represent a diverse group of individuals with significant between-subjects variability in which senses are impaired, and which outcome measures best capture these differences.

piezas.titulo: Postcentral cortical thickness reduction in trigeminal neuralgia: a whole-brain surface-based morphometry MRI study
piezas.resumenOriginal: IntroductionTrigeminal neuralgia (TN) is a neuropathic pain disorder characterized by paroxysmal unilateral facial pain evoked by innocuous cutaneous stimulation or manoeuvres. In classical and idiopathic TN, objective evidence of somatosensory system damage is often difficult to demonstrate. Neuroimaging studies suggest cortical structural alterations, though findings have been inconsistent, likely reflecting variability in case definitions and cortical measurement methodologies. We therefore investigated cortical thickness changes in a biologically homogeneous cohort of patients with right-sided TN using a whole-brain surface-based morphometry (SBM) approach.Methods60 patients with classical or idiopathic right-sided TN and 30 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent 3 T structural MRI. Cortical thickness was computed using FreeSurfer. Whole-brain vertex-wise group comparisons were performed using a General Linear Model (GLM) with a non-parametric permutation-based cluster-wise correction for multiple comparisons.ResultsCompared with controls, patients with TN showed significantly reduced cortical thickness in eight clusters. The largest and most significant cluster was located in the left postcentral gyrus. Additional clusters were identified in the bilateral insular-temporal regions, the right precentral-postcentral region, the right lateral occipital cortex, and the right parieto-occipital junction. Cortical thickness within significant clusters did not correlate with disease duration.ConclusionRight-sided TN is associated with focal cortical thinning involving both somatosensory and associative cortical regions. While involvement of insular, parietal, and occipital cortices is consistent with network-level structural reorganization observed in chronic pain conditions, thinning of the contralateral postcentral cortex may reflect central changes secondary to damage of primary trigeminal afferents.

piezas.titulo: Impaired cholinergic modulation of striatal spiny projection neurons in repetitive behaviors associated with TSHZ3-linked autism spectrum disorder
piezas.resumenOriginal: Alterations in central cholinergic systems are implicated in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). We previously identified TSHZ3 as an ASD-linked gene and provided evidence, from transgenic mouse models, supporting the view that striatal cholinergic interneurons (SCINs) are key players in the core ASD trait represented by repetitive behaviors (RBs). Indeed, conditional deletion of Tshz3 in cholinergic neurons (Chat-cKO model) results in RBs associated with reduced SCIN firing activity and decreased striatal cholinergic tone. Here we tackled the resulting adaptations in the striatal circuitry underlying RBs in Chat-cKO, focusing on the two populations of striatal projection neurons (SPNs) that express dopamine D1 (D1R) or D2 (D2R) receptor. Using patch-clamp electrophysiological recordings, as well as behavioral, pharmacological and molecular approaches, we show reduced cholinergic transmission through the muscarinic M1 receptor onto SPNs, with no changes in the functionality or expression of this receptor. Notably, we demonstrate a loss of the differential excitability of D1R- vs. D2R-SPNs. Finally, acute in vivo treatment with the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor donepezil significantly alleviates RBs in mutant mice. These findings point to dysfunction of SCINs as a pathological and druggable mechanism underlying RBs in Tshz3-linked ASD, and to altered SPN excitability as a critical contributor in the resulting pathophysiological functioning of the striatum.

piezas.titulo: The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought
piezas.resumenOriginal: A major new study reveals that autistic children’s brains process faces differently, and those differences may begin earlier than scientists previously thought. Researchers found that brain signals associated with recognizing faces become more specialized as neurotypical children grow older, but show much less change in autistic children. The discovery could help explain why some autistic people have difficulty recognizing faces and reading emotions.

Descripción INCIBE ha coordinado la publicación de una vulnerabilidad de severidad alta que afecta a WhatsApp for Dolibarr de Sgestion / EasySoft, un módulo de terceros que integra la mensajería de WhatsApp en Dolibarr. La vulnerabilidad ha sido descubierta por Gabriel Jesús Machado Tavares. A esta vulnerabilidad se le ha asignado el siguiente código, puntuación base CVSS v4.0, vector del CVSS y tipo de vulnerabilidad CWE: CVE-2026-76173: CVSS v4.0: 8.8 | CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:N/VA:L/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N | CWE-89 Solución El fabricante ha confirmado que el parche que corrige la vulnerabilidad ya ha sido desplegado. Detalle CVE-2026-76173 : vulnerabilidad de inyección SQL ciega en el endpoint público public/webhook/receiver.php del módulo WhatsApp para Dolibarr 1.9. El valor del número de teléfono derivado del parámetro data.key.remoteJid, recibido mediante una petición JSON, se incorpora a una consulta SQL sin escape ni parametrización. Con la opción WHATSAPP_WEBHOOK_ALLOW habilitada, un atacante remoto no autenticado podría manipular dicho parámetro para alterar la consulta. La explotación mediante una técnica basada en tiempos podría permitir obtener información de la base de datos y degradar el servicio. Rama 4.36.x, hasta 4.36.2F inclusive. Rama 4.35.x, hasta 4.35.6M inclusive. Rama 4.34.x, hasta 4.34.8M inclusive. Rama 4.33.x, hasta 4.33.10M inclusive. Ramas fuera de soporte, a partir de 4.25.1F. Arista incluye las series 710, 720D, 720XP/722XPM, 750X, 7010TX, 7020R/R4, 7130 con EOS, 7170, 7050X3/X4, 7060X/X2/X4/X5/X6/XE7, 7260X/X3, 7280R/R2/R3/R4, 7300X/X3, 7320X, 7358X4, 7368X4, 7388X5, 7500R/R2/R3 y 7800R3/R4, 7700R4, AWE 5000, AWE 7200R y ZTX-7200. Descripción Joshua Foote, de JP Morgan Chase, ha informado sobre 1 vulnerabilidad de severidad crítica en Arista EOS. También recomienda autenticar los pares BGP mediante TCP-AO para reducir la exposición. Consultar el boletín de Arista . Detalle CVE-2026-121289 : un desbordamiento de búfer en la pila al procesar un paquete BGP manipulado puede terminar el proceso del agente y cerrar todas sus sesiones. piezas.titulo: LEGaTO: Low-Energy Heterogeneous Computing Workshop
piezas.resumenOriginal: Workshops Friday, 04 September, 2020 LEGaTO is a three-year H2020 project on developing a toolset for low-energy heterogeneous computing that also considers fault tolerance, programmability and security. The project optimized a number of use cases for low-energy. The objective of the workshop is to apply the optimization low-energy techniques to other stakeholders in each of the project's use cases. Scope We are broadly looking to engage the Artificial Intelligence, Smart City, Smart Home, Helthcare and IOT communities to evangalize the low-energy optimization techniques that we have developed for these communities during the lifetime of the LEGaTO project. In particular, we will showcase how the heterogeneous low-energy small form-factor hardware could be coupled to an energy efficient runtime to produce one order of energy savings across these use cases. piezas.titulo: El malestar psicológico a través del inglés y otros idiomas
piezas.resumenOriginal: El malestar psicológico a través del inglés y otros idiomas emcamara 29/10/2026 26/11/2026 Fecha y hora: 26/11/26, 5pm CET Ponentes : Anna-Maria Bucur, Dalle Molle Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Università della Svizzera italiana (Italia) Presentador: Paolo Rosso, Universidad Politécnica de Valencia (España). Resumen: La presentación analiza cómo el procesamiento del lenguaje natural puede respaldar la investigación psicológica analizando interacciones procedentes de redes sociales para comprender mejor el malestar psicológico. Mientras que el PLN resulta eficaz a la hora de identificar patrones lingüísticos, la psicología articula la investigación definiendo los conceptos clave, explicando su relevancia y aportando un marco para interpretar los hallazgos. La ponencia comienza con varios estudios de caso centrados en la supervivencia al cáncer, la identificación de problemas de salud mental en la población general y la exploración de momentos de felicidad en personas diagnosticadas con depresión, todos ellos a partir de datos en inglés. A continuación, aborda consideraciones transculturales al trabajar con datos en idiomas distintos del inglés y evalúa los modelos del lenguaje de gran tamaño (LLM) para este fin. La presentación subraya que un PLN fundamentado en la teoría puede desvelar trayectorias psicológicas y ofrecer perspectivas valiosas para las intervenciones terapéuticas. No obstante, también destaca cómo la falta de datos de calidad y de evaluaciones adecuadas plantea retos a la hora de desarrollar métodos aplicables a lenguas más allá del inglés. Reseña: Ana-Maria Bucur es investigadora postdoctoral en el Instituto Dalle Molle de Inteligencia Artificial (IDSIA), Università della Svizzera italiana, donde trabaja en el Laboratorio de Recuperación de Información del profesor Fabio Crestani. Realizó un doctorado en cotutela entre la Universitat Politècnica de València y la Universidad de Bucarest, bajo la dirección de los profesores Paolo Rosso y Liviu P. Dinu. Ana-Maria ha participado en colaboraciones interdisciplinares que abarcan tanto la psicología como las humanidades digitales. Su investigación se centra principalmente en el procesamiento del lenguaje natural (PLN) aplicado a la salud mental, investigando en especial cómo las personas expresan sus estados psicológicos a través del lenguaje y de qué manera los métodos computacionales pueden mejorar nuestra comprensión de la salud mental y respaldar el bienestar. Más recientemente, ha estado explorando cómo influye la cultura en las manifestaciones de los trastornos mentales y cómo desarrollar métodos computacionales con sensibilidad cultural para un cribado de salud mental más inclusivo.
