piezas.titulo: Morpho-functional characterization of a putative direct ipsilateral corticospinal pathway in healthy adults: a single-pulse TMS study
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundIpsilateral motor-evoked potentials (iMEPs) elicited by transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) are attributed to indirect corticofugal pathways, particularly cortico-reticulospinal pathways. However, an uncrossed corticospinal component may allow some iMEPs to reflect faster, more direct transmission.ObjectiveTo distinguish non-CST-like iMEPs from responses compatible with a putative direct ipsilateral corticospinal component using a multidimensional TMS framework.MethodsTen right-handed adults underwent neuronavigated single-pulse TMS of primary motor cortex. Responses were recorded from biceps brachii, triceps brachii, flexor carpi radialis, extensor carpi radialis, and first dorsal interosseous, with 20 trials per muscle. Ipsilateral responses were assessed by iMEP/cMEP amplitude, latency difference, reproducibility, waveform correlation, hotspot distance, and startle modulation. CST-like responses met five criteria: Δ latency ≤2 ms, reproducibility ≥70%, waveform correlation ≥0.80, hotspot distance ≤10 mm, and startle facilitation <20%.ResultsiMEPs were detected in 20/50 muscle-level observations, most frequently in biceps brachii (70%). iMEP amplitude differed across muscles (Friedman χ2 = 11.45, p = 0.02199), with proximal and flexor predominance. Five responses in two participants met CST-like criteria, showing shorter latency differences (0.85 ± 0.40 vs. 5.61 ± 1.50 ms), higher reproducibility (84.0% vs. 61.7%), greater waveform similarity (r = 0.90 vs. 0.61), closer hotspot localization (6.26 vs. 19.58 mm), and minimal startle facilitation (2.58% vs. 49.31%). This multidimensional phenotype was not defined by response amplitude alone, supporting physiological heterogeneity rather than simple differences in response magnitude.ConclusionIn this exploratory cohort, iMEPs exhibited considerable physiological heterogeneity. Notably, five short-latency, reproducible responses displaying electrophysiological features resembling conventional cMEPs, including responses recorded from the FDI muscle, were identified in only two of the ten participants. Although these observations raise the possibility of a contribution from uncrossed corticospinal projections, they do not provide definitive evidence of the underlying descending pathway. Moreover, the small sample size and the concentration of these responses in a limited subset of participants preclude reliable inferences regarding their prevalence in the general population.

piezas.titulo: Cortical thinning and functional reorganization as well as related transcriptomic signatures during early motor recovery following acute basal ganglia ischemic stroke.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Background Acute basal ganglia ischemic stroke (ABGIS) commonly causes severe motor impairment, yet early spatiotemporal patterns of cortical morphological alterations and functional reorganization alongside the spatially coupled transcriptomic signatures remain unclear. Methods Twenty-six ABGIS patients and thirty-three normal controls (NCs) received multimodal MRI and neurological examinations, and patients were reassessed at 1-month follow-up. Cortical morphological changes and brain functional reorganization were analyzed based on cortical thickness (CT) and functional connectivity (FC). We identified the most discriminative FC features based on machine learning (ML) classification and interpretability analyses, and investigated transcriptomic signatures associated with FC alterations via the Allen Human Brain Atlas. Results No differences in CT were found between baseline ABGIS patients (ABGIS_1) and NCs. Compared with ABGIS_1, follow-up patients (ABGIS_2) exhibited reduced CT in the left postcentral gyrus (PoCG.L), left superior parietal lobule (SPL.L), and left supramarginal gyrus (SMG.L). Compared with NCs, ABGIS_1 showed decreased FC from PoCG.L/SPL.L to sensorimotor cortex and occipital cortex. ABGIS_2 presented elevated FC relative to ABGIS_1 between PoCG.L and the right precentral gyrus (PreCG.R), and between SPL.L and the bilateral precentral gyrus as well as right superior occipital gyrus. Longitudinal increases in FC between PoCG.L/SPL.L and PreCG.R were positively correlated with improvements in Fugl-Meyer Assessment scores. ML models coupled with interpretability analyses preliminarily demonstrated that FC between PoCG.L/SPL.L and PreCG.R made prominent contributions to classification. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that gene sets correlated with FC alterations were mainly enriched in neuronal synaptic structure and synaptic signaling, chromatin regulation, as well as DNA and RNA metabolism. Conclusions This study verifies progressive cortical thinning and adaptive functional reorganization during early motor recovery following ABGIS, with such brain functional alterations paralleling distinct transcriptomic signatures, providing neuropathological and spatial transcriptomic clues for interpreting early motor recovery.

piezas.titulo: Larch: Learned Query Optimization for Semantic Predicates
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2606.07923v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: With the advent of Large Language Models (LLMs), many database systems introduced semantic operators that enabled analytical queries over unstructured data (e.g. text, images, videos). Semantic operators typically incur high inference costs and latencies making semantic (AI) SQL queries challenging to apply on large scale datasets. At the same time, their semantic nature leads database engines to treat them as black boxes, making AISQL queries difficult to optimize. In this paper, we introduce Larch, a framework for optimizing the execution of semantic filters in AI SQL queries. Larch was inspired by two key observations: i) the high latency of semantic operators leaves significant room for computationally-heavy runtime optimization techniques, ii) unstructured data are typically accompanied by semantic information in the form of embeddings allowing for efficient semantic comparisons between AI_FILTER prompts and data values. Based on these two key observations, we present two Larch variants: Larch-A2C and Larch-Sel. Larch-A2C encodes arbitrary semantic filters expression tree using an embedding-augmented Gated Graph Neural Network and formulates the filter evaluation order as a Markov decision process. In contrast, Larch-Sel leverages a supervised learning model to predict filter selectivities, subsequently applying dynamic programming to find a near-optimal evaluation order for each input row. Evaluated across diverse real-world datasets and comprehensive synthetic workloads, both Larch variants always outperform existing semantic filter optimization techniques in terms of token usage on every dataset and workload. Our results demonstrate that Larch is robust across diverse workloads across text and image modalities, 6%--30% lower total token costs and 3x--19x lower token costs overhead than Palimpzest and Quest.

piezas.titulo: Disentangling Forgetting from Utility: Lightweight LLM Unlearning via Orthogonal Null-Space Projection
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2611.17864v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) pose significant security risks by retaining private or hazardous information, creating an urgent need for unlearning techniques that excise specific knowledge without compromising general utility. However, prevailing fine-tuning-based unlearning methods struggle to achieve this balance, often suffering from computational inefficiency and unintended utility degradation due to the entangled nature of knowledge within model parameters. To disentangle forgetting from utility, we propose UUE, a theoretically grounded framework that reformulates unlearning as controllable model editing. First, UUE projects parameter updates into the orthogonal left null space of retained knowledge representations, strictly ensuring that the editing process causes minimal interference to the model's general capabilities. Second, distinct from targeted mapping, we introduce a convex untargeted objective that derives a closed-form analytical solution to effectively disrupt undesired knowledge by pushing forget-set embeddings toward their antipodal points. We implement UUE via lightweight, pluggable adapters (including a low-rank variant, UUE-L), enabling efficient deployment without modifying the frozen backbone. Extensive experiments on TOFU and WMDP benchmarks demonstrate that UUE and UUE-L achieve superior unlearning efficacy, significantly outperforming existing methods.

piezas.titulo: Peer Mentoring Benefits in Rehabilitation for Individuals With Spinal Cord Injury: A Systematic Review.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Importance The lived experiences of peer mentors with spinal cord injury (SCI) provide distinct value in the rehabilitation process and contribute to improved outcomes. When combined with traditional therapy, peer mentorship programs can enhance life satisfaction among individuals living with SCI. Objective To explore the impact that peer-led mentorship programs and interventions have on the rehabilitation outcomes for individuals with a spinal cord injury (SCI). Data sources PubMed, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, ERIC, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, MedNar, and OpenGrey were searched between 2014 and 2024. The Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool was adapted and used to assess risk of bias in the included studies. Study selection and data collection Inclusion criteria included individuals with SCI who participated in peer mentorship and reported outcomes on quality of life, well-being, independence, or activities of daily living (ADLs) or instrumental ADLs. Exclusion criteria included interventions conducted via telehealth or reported outcomes of social participation. Findings Five articles were analyzed for synthesis, which included individuals 18 yr and older with an SCI. Findings support peer mentorship as an important component of rehabilitation. Findings may have limited generalizability across different settings and populations because of the small number of available studies and variability in study designs, interventions, and outcome measures. None of the articles reviewed included occupational therapists. Conclusions and relevance This review highlighted the benefits of peer mentorship in enhanced life satisfaction. Findings support peer mentorship as an important component of rehabilitation. Future research should examine the benefits of incorporating peer-led intervention programs across the continuum of care, including occupational therapy, in enhancing best practices in SCI rehabilitation. Plain-Language Summary: Peer mentorship programs can help people with spinal cord injuries adjust to daily life by providing guidance, support, and encouragement that professionals without lived experience may not offer. This review found that peer mentoring can improve psychological well-being and health management and reduce unplanned hospital visits. Evidence is limited because of the small number of studies and variations in study design; however, the results suggest that meaningful benefits may be present. Further research is needed to determine the most effective way to implement peer mentorship across rehabilitation settings.

piezas.titulo: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum
piezas.resumenOriginal: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum STAR Admin Thu, 06/15/2017 - 14:07 STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder (SPD) and T.A.C.T. (Teaching the Autism Community Trades) are two Colorado nonprofits who have partnered to create a series of respite camps serving adolescents who have autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Developmental Pathways has awarded the organizations a $25,000 grant to fund three F.U.S.E. (Fostering Unlimited Success and Empowerment) camps through 2018. STAR Institute offers premier treatment for SPD and brings expertise in social skills while T.AC.T. teaches trade and life skills to individuals with ASD and SPD with an emphasis on fostering independence and personal growth. “This is a very rare and exciting way to see two nonprofits interact. Our partnership to create F.U.S.E. allows both of our organizations to combine expertise in a way that best serves these adolescents to find new interests and gain the soft skills to successfully participate in peer groups and future workplaces”, says Dick Layton, Director of STAR Institute for SPD. The respite camps will be week-long day camps that host six students per camp ages 12-15 who have autism spectrum disorder. The camps will teach pre-vocational and vocational skills in a supportive, social, and inclusionary environment. Each camp has a different project for participants including: building a non-motorized go-cart with a partner, building an instrument to play in a band, and crafting board games. “The intended focus of F.U.S.E. is not just about offering a respite program for families. By generating new experiences for these adolescents, we hope to foster new skills, new interests, develop social skills, and give them a sense of empowerment to participate in what hopefully becomes a new hobby or future career interest”, says Danny Combs co-founder and president of T.A.C.T. SPD is a neurological disorder that disrupts the way an individual processes and responds to sensations. The disorder can affect people in only one sense–for example, just touch or just sight or just movement–or in multiple senses. One person with SPD may over-respond to touch sensation and find clothing, physical contact, other tactile sensory input to be unbearable and/or they may respond to visual or auditory or another sensory input. Another person might under-respond and show little or no reaction to stimulation, even pain or extreme hot and cold or just may be slow to respond to sensation. SPD and ASD have a high co-morbidity rate, but are also found to be standalone disorders. ASD refers to conditions categorized by challenges with social skills, repetitive behaviors, speech and nonverbal communication, as well as by unique strengths and differences that can occur on a range from mild to severe. Individuals with ASD and SPD frequently struggle with interpersonal skills over their lifetime and are often underestimated, which can lead to specific difficulty in career and relationships. F.U.S.E. aims to give individuals the ability to ignite new interests and feel empowered in group collaboration, which can lead to greater success in career and relationships. About STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder: The STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder, a Colorado 501(c)(3), is the world leader in treatment, research, and education for Sensory Processing Disorder, a neurological condition that disrupts the daily lives of more than 4 million Americans. The STAR Institute is the premier treatment center for children, adults and families living with Sensory Processing Disorder, feeding disorders, and other sensory conditions associated with ADHD, autism, and other developmental disorders. Dr. Lucy Jane Miller, founder of STAR Institute, is widely recognized as the leader in Sensory Processing Disorder research worldwide. For more information about the Greenwood Village, Colorado clinic, visit http://www.spdSTAR.org or call 303-221-7827. About T.A.C.T. (Teaching the Autism Community Trades): T.A.C.T is a 501(c)(3) that provides trade and technical skills to children, young adults and families living with Autism Spectrum Disorder. Early vocational training helps young adults before they leave high school and sets them up for long term success. Our programs are designed to empower individuals and develop interests and skills for life. To learn more visit: https://tactkids.org or call 720-460-0897. About Developmental Pathways: Developmental Pathways is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit agency serving individuals with developmental disabilities/delays and their families. We are also one of Colorado’s Community Centered Boards (CCB) connecting people to federal, state, county, and private funding in Arapahoe County, Douglas County, and the City of Aurora. We passionately believe inclusion is for everyone and offer services through Home and Community Based Medicaid Waiver programs, locally funded programs, and partnerships with other community organizations. piezas.titulo: Hormone therapy attenuates menopause-related impairments in motor cortical spike-timing-dependent plasticity
piezas.resumenOriginal: The menopause marks the permanent cessation of menstruation via a decline in endogenous hormone production. This transition influences brain health, yet its effects on motor cortical excitability and spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) are poorly understood. Across two sites, 46 females were categorised as pre-menopausal (PRE, age 28{+/-}7 years), perimenopausal (PERI, 50{+/-}3 years), post-menopausal (POST, 60{+/-}8 years), or combined continuous hormone therapy users (HT, 52{+/-}3 years). Transcranial magnetic stimulation was used to measure corticospinal excitability (MEP/Mmax), short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI), and intracortical facilitation (ICF) before, then 10 and 30 min after a paired associative stimulation (PAS) protocol (25-ms interstimulus interval). Serum hormone concentrations were quantified from venous blood. Resting corticospinal excitability and SICI were not different between groups before the PAS protocol. However, a group x time interaction (p=0.0152) for MEP/Mmax revealed distinct STDP responses. PRE showed a significant increase in corticospinal excitability following PAS (+48%, p=0.0045), whereas PERI and POST showed no facilitation (p[≥]0.2079). Between groups, both PRE and HT exceeded PERI, and HT also exceeded POST; however, HT users showed a smaller, non-significant increase (+32%, p=0.0666) that collectively distinguished them from the blunted responses of PERI and POST. The magnitude of STDP was not associated with any single hormone or chronological age across the whole sample of participants. These findings provide the first evidence that motor cortical STDP is influenced by menopause stage. With blunted responses in PERI and POST, yet preserved responses in HT users, these data have implications for motor learning and rehabilitation across the female adult lifespan.

piezas.titulo: Identifying and Mitigating API Misuse in Large Language Models
piezas.resumenOriginal: arXiv:2503.22821v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: API misuse in code generated by large language models (LLMs) presents a serious and growing challenge in software development, as although LLMs demonstrate impressive code generation capabilities, their interactions with complex library APIs are often error-prone and can lead to software failures and vulnerabilities. In this paper, we conduct a large-scale study of API misuse patterns in LLM-generated code by analyzing both method selection and parameter usage across Python and Java, using three representative LLMs: StarCoder-7B, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, and GitHub Copilot. Based on extensive manual annotation of 3,209 method-level and 3,492 parameter-level misuses, we identify and categorize four recurring misuse types by building on and refining prior API misuse taxonomies. Our evaluation of the three LLMs reveals persistent challenges in API usage, particularly hallucination and intent misalignment. To address these issues, we propose Dr.Fix, an LLM-based automatic repair approach guided by our taxonomy, which improves repair accuracy compared to baseline prompting and existing repair methods, achieving gains of up to 38.4 BLEU and up to 72 more exact matches on benchmark datasets. This work offers important insights into the current limitations of LLMs in API usage and points to directions for improving automated misuse repair in code generation systems.

piezas.titulo: Fragments: October 21
piezas.resumenOriginal: Gergely Orosz is frustrated at those that entered his explicitly “No AI” essay competition and used AI. He goes on to say: When I start to suspect some part is AI about someone I don’t know: how can I tell how much of it is? And how much time and effort do I want to invest to figure out? I fear most people do not realize this last part: that when it takes time and effort from others to figure out what % is AI, and what % is YOU, then I will simply assume it’s probably 100% AI and 0% you So when producing anything that is meant for other humans, if you use even a little AI, you risk the assumption that it is all AI and pointless to pay attention to In general, I agree with him, and react much the same. Once I hear LLM Voice, I flip the bozo bit and check out of the post. But as I do this I have caveats. How accurate is my neural net at AI-detection, are humans taking on AI-ish elements in their normal communication? And more seriously there are some valid uses for AI. Jim Highsmith’s story of his second brain helping him deal with Parkinson’s is one. Another is folks who don’t know English well, using AI to translate. Am I being unfair when I flip the AI voice bit when I read/listen to them? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I was sad to hear that the Grace Hopper Celebration is canceled this year. It’s an event run by Anitab.org to promote women and non-binary technologists in the software industry. Many of my colleagues have been encouraged and inspired by going to this event, which makes a refreshing change to what is often a male-dominated world. It seems the current crusade against diversity initiatives has had a big impact on funding. We are still a long way from where we should be on gender diversity in our profession, and losing an event like this only makes things more difficult. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I’ve always found Cindy Sridharan’s writing to be worth reading, and she’s broken a quiet period with a monster of an article: How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code . Since Medium estimates it as a 64 minute read, I didn’t jump in lightly, but settled down on a flight from Amsterdam to Stuttgart. I’m glad I did, because there’s lot of good material in there, and I’d struggle to find anything to cut. In the article she uses three recent bug hunts to surface principles for how to best use an AI tool for debugging. Much of this is governed by this wise observation: Agents are not humans. They’re far more capable than humans when it comes to many things, and we should be leaning into these strengths, rather than trying to get agents to replicate human patterns of problem solving which might be suboptimal in agentic contexts. One conclusion from her experiences is that the code often isn’t the best thing for agents to look at having an agent start an investigation by first reading the code is an anti-pattern. In fact, reading the code first to formulate hypotheses about a bug should always be the very last resort of the agentic investigation process, not the starting point. An agent should first collect all available evidence about the bug, and only then formulate the hypotheses from the code that might best explain what’s being observed. She distinguishes between a bottom tier of facts: raw data that agent can find about the behavior of the system - and an upper tier of hypotheses: inferences that the agents make based on that data. Diagnosing a bug now becomes a problem of finding the hypothesis in the top tier that satisfies every fact from the bottom tier. The agents need to be steered towards the hypotheses that are the likest cause of the bug and then subject these hypotheses to validation. She has a three-step process to do this. First she identifies the most important facts, the signals that might explain or identify the bug. The factual tier has many data points. Not all of them are equally valuable. In fact, some of it might be active noise that doesn’t help an agent to be steered towards most promising hypothesis. The agent first needs to identify the data points in the factual tier that are actually related to the bug. Agents do this best when they are given a high-quality control A control is a behavior of the system that doesn’t exhibit the bug. This may be requests that trigger the bug compared to those that don’t, or different builds of the product, or the same build in different environments. With signals highlighted, she then focuses on the hypotheses that are most promising, because they fit best with the signals. A hypothesis should satisfy all the facts, the most valuable signals are those that are only satisfied by a few hypotheses. A table of hypotheses and signals helps visualize the strength of the signals and the likelihood of the hypotheses. The third step is then validating the promising hypotheses against every fact, treating each fact as constraint on the solution. Across the three bugs chronicled in this post, my most valuable contributions weren’t knowledge of the code. They were picking a control, choosing a constraint, and rejecting a hypothesis that hadn’t been validated. The engineers who thrive in an agent-native world will be the ones who are good at designing such verification loops, whether or not they understand the code it verifies. This directing has to remember the opening point that agents have different capabilities to humans. A human wants to deal with less data. All abstractions we currently have (aggregation, visualizations etc) are designed to help humans deal with less data. An agent, however, needs more raw data; its strength lies in processing huge volumes of data at a rapid clip. Aggregation — the thing that makes a dashboard useful to a human — is often the thing that destroys the value of the signal for an agent Agents’ ability to consume lots of raw data also affects how we build systems. More logging gives agents more data to chew on. And thus far, the human is still necessary to direct the agent In each of the three bugs chronicled in this post, the agent was more than capable of getting to the root cause by itself, but it didn’t do so. It didn’t set up a control in the “latency bug” until I asked it to While it’s a long post, it’s engagingly written and full of useful details. I hope my little summary encourages you to give it the read it deserves.

piezas.titulo: Validation of the Hungarian version of the Coma Recovery Scale-Revised in patients with disorders of consciousness
piezas.resumenOriginal: ObjectiveOur objective was to validate the Hungarian version of the Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R).DesignWe conducted a multicenter study across neurology, intensive care, neuro-rehabilitation, and nursing departments in Hungary. Thirty-one patients (17 males; mean age 49.1 ± 16.1 years) with disorders of consciousness (DOC) following severe acquired brain injury were assessed. Two independent raters reassessed the same patients within a one-week window to evaluate inter-rater and intra-rater reliability. We assessed reliability using weighted Cohen’s Kappa and evaluated concurrent validity using Spearman’s rank correlation.ResultsConcurrent validity with the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) was strong across all raters and time points (rho = 0.882–0.934, p < 0.001). Inter-rater reliability for the total score was excellent at initial assessment (wk = 0.977) and remained high at follow-up (wk = 0.977). Diagnostic classification agreement between raters was nearly perfect (wk = 0.936–1.000).ConclusionThe Hungarian CRS-R is a valid and reliable instrument that preserves the robustness of the original version. Its implementation fills a critical gap in national healthcare by providing an evidence-based tool to reduce DOC misdiagnosis rates.

piezas.titulo: AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security
piezas.resumenOriginal: This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast . Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance. However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof? There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP? Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces. Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces. This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution. Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust. How quickly can de-authentication attacks occur? An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system. There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals? Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform. Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration. The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents. Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability. Does true zero-trust architecture exist? The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist? Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub , we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system. We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policies rather than trusting the third-party agentic service providers. Additionally, trust in services is presented by ensuring constraints around their service models where agentic activities are tracked and managed via logs including management of their token revocation list to avoid replay attacks depending on the type of application. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. Things like balancing the adversarial accuracy along with certified adversarial robustness can help to determine how much the model can be trusted. But the question is, can we settle for anything less than foolproof when it comes to deployment of agents in the real world? And if so, how much impact can be controlled, and who is responsible for the remaining component? References Wickremasinghe G, Sandjaja FR, Rafferty K, Sharma V. piezas.titulo: Effects of resistance training on neuronal response to visual food cues in adults with overweight/obesity.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Background Individuals with overweight/obesity show altered neuronal response to food cues, but how exercise affects this response remains unclear. This study examined resistance training (RT) effects on neuronal response to visual food cues and eating behaviors in adults with overweight/obesity. We hypothesized RT would be associated with decreased response in brain regions involved in regulating energy intake and decreased ad libitum intake, with brain and behavioral changes correlated. Exploratory analyses evaluated RT effects on eating behaviors and whole-brain response and compared RT with a 12-week diet intervention. Methods Participants (N = 19) completed a visual food cues task during functional magnetic resonance imaging in fasted and fed states, before and after a 12-week RT program. Paired t-tests examined RT effects on response to high-calorie foods versus non-food objects in regions of interest (ROIs; dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, insula, nucleus accumbens), energy intake, Three Factor Eating Questionnaire, and whole-brain response. Repeated measures correlations examined associations between changes in ROIs and energy intake. Linear mixed models compared RT and diet (N = 17). Results RT was associated with decreased dietary disinhibition (p = 0.009) and increased restraint (p = 0.023). No significant within-group effects were observed on neuronal response, energy intake, or associations between the two. Between-group analyses demonstrated (1) increased restraint across groups (p = 0.017), with a stronger effect for diet, and (2) a significant group*time interaction in right posterior insula and left primary somatosensory cortex (p Conclusions Despite an absence of observed changes in predefined ROIs or energy intake, RT may promote self-regulatory eating behaviors in adults with overweight/obesity. Exploratory analyses suggest RT and diet may have distinct effects on neuronal response to food cues, with RT decreasing and diet increasing response in interoceptive and sensory processing regions. Findings should be interpreted with caution, however, given the small, non-randomized sample. Clinical trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers: NCT02047721 and NCT03985787.

piezas.titulo: Validity and Reliability of the Activity Card Sort 3 in Persons With Thumb Carpometacarpal Osteoarthritis.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceAlthough individuals with thumb carpometacarpal (CMC1) osteoarthritis (OA) commonly experience participation restrictions, participation-focused outcome measures remain underinvestigated, and clinicians primarily rely on assessments of impairments in body structures and functions.ObjectiveTo determine the concurrent validity, test-retest reliability, and precision of the Activity Card Sort 3 (ACS3) in individuals with nonoperative CMC1 OA.DesignSingle-cohort observational psychometric study with repeated measures over a 2-week interval.SettingRemote assessments conducted via videoconferencing.ParticipantsThirty-three adults with radiographically confirmed CMC1 OA completed two virtual assessments approximately 2 weeks apart.Outcomes and MeasuresConcurrent validity was examined by comparing ACS3 domain and total scores with the World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0 (WHODAS 2.0). Test-retest reliability of the "current," "previous," and "% retained" activities scores was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC 3,1 ). Precision was assessed using the standard error of measurement and minimal detectable change.ResultsThe ACS3 demonstrated good concurrent validity through strong associations with conceptually related WHODAS 2.0 domains. "Current" and "% retained" scores demonstrated good-to-excellent test-retest reliability across all domains. "Current" scores consistently showed the highest reliability and precision. "Previous" scores demonstrated lower reliability and greater measurement error, suggesting recall bias. Carrying forward "previous" scores from session 1 to session 2 improved the reliability of "% retained" scores.Conclusions and RelevanceThe ACS3 is a valid and reliable measure of participation for individuals with nonoperative CMC1 OA. The "current" and "% retained" scores may support occupational therapy practitioners in conducting participation-focused assessment of persons with CMC1 OA.

piezas.titulo: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video
piezas.resumenOriginal: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works. The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below: We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...] As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention . Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...] The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units. Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself , allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster. We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues , where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments. piezas.titulo: Early mobilization and sleep quality in critically ill patients: a narrative review
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundSufficient and high-quality sleep is widely regarded as a key factor in maintaining both physical and mental health. However, critically ill patients experience severe sleep disruption and profound circadian deregulation, which are driven by both the severity of illness and the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) environment. Early mobilization and rehabilitation in ICU are widely recognized as safe, feasible and pivotal interventions, that have been directly linked to improved post-ICU neuropsychiatric outcomes and more effective delirium control.AimThe purpose of this review is to summarize the current knowledge on the impact of early mobilization (EM) in critical care patients on their sleep quality and architecture.MethodsThis is a narrative review that critically examines studies indexed on PubMed since 2021, referring to the effect of physiotherapy on sleep in the ICU.ResultsEarly mobilization and rehabilitation of critical care patients have been demonstrated to act as a successful neuroprotective intervention, capable of modifying post-ICU neuropsychiatric outcomes and preventing or minimizing the severity of delirium. Moreover, it has been reported that these interventions improve cognitive and functional impairments, reduce ICU-related anxiety, and decrease the frequency of Post-Intensive Care Syndrome (PICS). However, robust evidence of their effect on sleep-specific outcomes remains limited due to the scarcity, small sample size and heterogeneity of existing studies.ConclusionCurrent evidence suggests physiotherapy and EM may improve sleep quality; however, there is insufficient data to draw definitive conclusions about the effect of EM on sleep in critical care patients.

destilado.texto: Mover a los pacientes pronto parece aliviar la ansiedad y el delirio en unidades de cuidados intensivos. La revisión de Frontiers in Neurology indica que la fisioterapia y la early mobilization podrían mejorar la sleep quality, aunque los estudios son pocos y variados. ¿Podrá la práctica rutinaria confirmar este beneficio?

piezas.titulo: Partially shared representational space for vision and language across objects, scenes, and visual events
piezas.resumenOriginal: Deep neural networks (DNNs) and behavioural similarity judgements of visual stimuli predict neural responses in visual cortex. Recent work shows that large language model (LLM) embeddings and similarity judgements of language descriptions also predict visual brain activity. These predictors were examined separately across modalities (vision vs language) and types (models vs human behaviour). It remains unclear to what extent these predictors explain shared or unique aspects of visual brain responses, how these contributions vary along the visual hierarchy and category-selective regions, and whether vision-language convergence depends on the stimulus type. We used three fMRI datasets progressing toward naturalistic visual experience, from objects (THINGS) to scenes (NSD) to dynamic events (BMD). For each dataset, we collected similarity judgements of visual stimuli and of their language descriptions from human participants (N = 21-35), extracted vision DNN features and LLM embeddings, and related similarity judgements and model representations to visual brain responses using representational similarity analysis (RSA) and variance partitioning. Vision-language convergence was higher within behaviour than within models. From objects to dynamic events, LLM alignment with vision-based similarity judgements increased, whereas vision DNN alignment remained stable. A shared, predominantly cross-modal component increased along the visual hierarchy and dominated explained variance in high-level visual cortex. LLMs made their largest unique contributions in face- and body-selective regions (FFA and EBA), where shared representations of vision- and language-based human similarity judgements also explained variance beyond the models. In summary, we find a partially shared representational space for vision and language in high-level visual cortex, most clearly in regions representing social information related to people and their actions. As each predictor retained unique variance, combining computational models and human behaviour across vision and language may offer a more comprehensive account of high-level visual representations.

piezas.titulo: The role of the right temporal lobe in neural network mechanisms during working memory encoding
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundVisual working memory (vWM) impairment is common in patients with temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) and is more severe in those with right TLE (RTLE), suggesting the significant role of right temporal lobe in WM processes.MethodsWe recruited patients with left TLE (LTLE group, n = 20), RTLE (RTLE group, n = 20) and 35 healthy controls (Control), and examined their vWM performance while simultaneously recording task-based EEG. The alterations in the neural oscillations and neural network were analyzed during the WM encoding phase. In addition, we examined the relationship between the neural oscillations and WM performance, as well as the relationship between the neural network and WM performance, to further explore the role of the right temporal lobe in WM encoding.ResultsRemarkably lower accuracy (both p < 0.001) and significantly longer response times (LTLE vs. Control: p = 0.026; RTLE vs. Control: p < 0.001) were found in both LTLE and RTLE groups compared with controls. The RTLE group experienced notably delayed response time in comparison to the LTLE group (p = 0.026). In comparison to the LTLE group, the RTLE group displayed reduced theta power spectral density for the frontal (p = 0.024) and occipital (p = 0.011) regions, along with the Fz channel (p = 0.047). DTFF_outflow and DTFFz_outflow values in the RTLE group displayed reduction relative to the LTLE group (DTFF_outflow:p = 0.026; DTFFz_outflow: p = 0.037). The LTLE group showed weakened information flow from Fz to P3 (IFFz → P3, ANOVA, F = 3.45, p = 0.037; LSD, LTLE vs. Control: p = 0.013), whereas the RTLE group exhibited weakened information flow from Fz to P4 (IFFz → P4; ANOVA, F = 3.78, p = 0.028; LSD, RTLE vs. Control: p = 0.029), Fz to T4 (IFFz → T4; ANOVA, F = 4.67, p = 0.012; LSD, RTLE vs. Control: p = 0.009), and Fz to TP8 (IFFz → TP8; ANOVA, F = 3.11, p = 0.050; LSD, RTLE vs. Control: p = 0.017), which were positively associated with accuracy and inversely associated with response time.ConclusionAbnormal information transfer from the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex to the superior parietal lobe during the encoding phase may causes WM deficits; damage to information transfer from the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex to the right middle temporal and right inferior temporal gyri exacerbates WM impairments.

Pacientes con epilepsia del lóbulo temporal derecho mostraron menor precisión y menor potencia theta en regiones frontales y occipitales. ¿Podría entrenar esa zona mejorar la memoria?

piezas.titulo: Triboelectric Sensory Intelligence: From Mechanical Information Encoding to In-Sensor Memory, Neuromorphic Computing, and Closed-Loop Interaction.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Triboelectric interfaces are progressing beyond self-powered sensing toward integrated sensory systems capable of encoding, retaining, transforming, and responding to mechanical information. Yet, the rapid convergence of triboelectric transduction with memory, neuromorphic devices, and intelligent interfaces has also blurred the distinctions between signal generation, state modulation, physical computation, and task-level intelligence. This Review establishes an information-centric framework for triboelectric sensory intelligence, in which mechanical interaction is traced through electrical encoding, signal-device coupling, internal state evolution, sensory processing, perception, and ultimately closed-loop action. Sensory representations based on amplitude, polarity, temporal structure, spatial patterns, material-dependent responses, and multimodal signals are considered in terms of encoding fidelity, separability, and robustness. Stateful mechanisms based on resistive switching, charge storage, ferroelectric polarization, and ionic or electrochemical dynamics are then related to sensory memory, temporal filtering, synaptic plasticity, event-based transformation, and other physical computational primitives. Emphasis is placed on distinguishing structural integration from processing location, device dynamics from implemented computation, and hardware processing from downstream software inference. The Review further links these principles to tactile and material perception, gesture and motion interfaces, multisensory integration, and sensory-motor feedback, while introducing system-level considerations of reproducibility, energy, latency, scalability, and generalization. Looking forward, reliable source-receiver co-design, adaptive processing, scalable heterogeneous integration, and closed-loop operation will be central to translating triboelectric interfaces from isolated device demonstrations into persistent and autonomous sensory systems.

piezas.titulo: How Top-Down Are We? Reconsidering the Gap Between Occupational Therapy's Identity and Practice.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Occupational therapy has spent more than a century defining occupation as its professional core. Yet studies across countries and settings show a recurring gap. Therapists value occupation-centered practice while often relying on impairment-focused assessment and intervention. This article argues that the profession may face a translation problem more than an identity problem. Biomedical service structures, standardized measurement, workplace culture, and professional socialization can pull reasoning toward body functions. Bottom-up methods are not inherently incompatible with occupational therapy; the problem arises when change in a component is treated as sufficient evidence of occupational success. Drawing on occupational therapy research, the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, rehabilitation science, and disability rights, we argue that occupation and participation should remain the outcomes that organize assessment, intervention, and evaluation. Practical changes are proposed for clinical reasoning, outcome measurement, education, supervision, and service design.
